Not a fit for readers who want the rating to mean something objective, who need a working support mailbox before they pay, or who would rather not involve a face at all - the free scan keeps the photo on the device, but the colour analysis and every try-on require sending a compressed copy to the vendor and its model providers.
summary: TheFaceRating turns one selfie into a face rating. Google's MediaPipe face mesh places 478 landmarks in the browser, the site levels the head on the iris line and scores 11 proportions into a single 0-100 harmony number, then names the face shape across six prototypes and shows symmetry, canthal tilt, facial thirds and width-to-height ratio against a reference band. It also returns a celebrity bone-structure 'twin' as a percentage. The free scan needs no account, and we confirmed by running it that the measuring step sends nothing: landmarks, ratios and the result page are produced with no outbound request. The paid report adds 14 try-on renders on the buyer's own photo - six hairstyles, four necklines, four eyewear frames - plus a 12-season colour palette, a styling guide and, on Pro and VIP, a 30-day plan, a PDF and Studio credits for rating any look you find. Colour analysis is the one step that needs the photo, and the site asks for it with an unticked consent choice that can be declined while still returning full geometry results. Reports are sold by Vban LLC, a Wyoming company, under Wyoming law.

name: CCC (Claude Command Center)
pricing: Free: USD 0, with no tiers, no paid plan, no seat count and no account for the local app. Licensed FSL-1.1-MIT (copyright 2026 Amir Fish), which is source-available rather than OSI open source: you may use, copy, modify and redistribute it for any Permitted Purpose, a Competing Use is barred, and each version converts to the MIT license on its second anniversary. Downloads are a 3.6 MB notarized and Apple-signed DMG, a Homebrew tap (amirfish1/tap/ccc), a curl installer for macOS/Linux and a PowerShell installer for Windows. The optional CCC Cloud phone relay is account-based; no price appears for it on any fetched page either. No page on the site carries a price token other than $0.
best_for: Developers who already run several coding agents and keep losing track of them in terminal tabs. CCC is worth a look if you launch Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and friends from a terminal and want one local board that shows every session, which one is waiting on you, and which has quietly run out of context - without routing your work through someone else's cloud. It is not a fit for a single-session user (a terminal is enough), for anyone who wants a hosted team product with accounts and permissions, for a Windows or Linux shop expecting parity with the macOS app, or for a buyer who needs a company entity and a governing-law clause before installing software.
summary: CCC (Claude Command Center) is a local dashboard for people running several coding agents at once. Instead of owning execution, it reads each engine's on-disk state as the source of truth, so a session you started in a terminal, resumed by hand or launched headless outside the dashboard still shows up on the board - that is the difference between a dashboard and a second place you have to remember to work from. On top of the board it adds a needs-attention lane that flags sessions ending on a real question, a per-session context meter, plan-usage and rate-limit projections, a Kanban with a project tree and an infinite Flow canvas, group chats between agents, a work queue with verify-to-close receipts, git worktrees per task, and an optional fallback that keeps a limit-hit session running on a $0 model. The stack is deliberately plain: a stdlib-only Python server bound to 127.0.0.1 and a no-build vanilla-JS UI, with readable JSON state under ~/.claude/command-center/. Claude Code is first-class; Codex, Cursor, Antigravity, Kilo Code, Kimi Code, OpenCode and Devin spawn and ingest with documented gaps. Version 5.39.0 shipped 2026-10-18 and the repository was pushed the same day this review was written.

best_for: Writers and researchers who already have a finished Word or PowerPoint file and need the file itself changed - AI phrasing reduced, references converted to a target style, a document cut to a word limit, or a layout-preserving translation - then downloaded again as an editable DOCX or PPTX. Not a fit for anyone who wants a draft written for them (there is no generation entry point), for non-English humanizing, for assessed work where the institution restricts AI assistance, or for a buyer who needs a named company, country, postal address or a governing law that names a jurisdiction.
summary: HumanPen is a document toolbox that works on files rather than on a text box. You upload a DOCX or PPTX and get the same format back, edited: an AI-phrasing rewriter with two strengths that can import your own Turnitin or iThenticate report and touch only the flagged passages, a citation-format converter covering 12 styles, a shortener that hits a target word count, and a translator for 12 languages that keeps layout, charts and formulas. Billing is metered - you are charged for words actually rewritten, not for the whole file - and credits do not expire, so a 500-word job costs cents instead of a month's subscription. The humanizer is English-only and the vendor says so. There is also a documented REST API, an MCP server and an agent skill. The site is candid to an unusual degree about what the tool is for: the /ethics page states plainly that the humanizer is used to lower detector scores, declines to promise a pass, declines to run its own detector, and the Terms forbid submitting work as your own where an assessment requires independent work.

summary: Microsoft’s AI assistant for workplace productivity, search, writing, meetings, and enterprise software workflows.

name: Money Tracker (Expense & Budget)
pricing: Free with ads: manual entry, categories, budgets, charts, reports, multi-currency, split (AA) books and exports all work without paying. Premium is sold only inside the app stores - the vendor's own site publishes no price anywhere in its 45 locales. Apple's listing shows Yearly Premium $29.99 and Monthly Premium $2.99; Google Play lists in-app purchases at $2.99-$29.00 per item. Premium removes ads and adds unlimited AI entry, bill import (CSV, Excel, PDF or images), Android Smart Notification Entry, app lock, more books and accounts, and team books.
best_for: People who will log spending themselves - by hand, by voice, by photographing a receipt, or on Android by confirming a captured bank notification - and who want budgets and category reports without handing a bank login to an app. Fits solo users and small shared households that want one ledger, multiple currencies and split bills. Not a fit for anyone who needs a documented privacy notice covering financial data, a Terms of Service, or a named AI processor before installing a finance app.
summary: Money Tracker is a mobile expense tracker and budget app for Android and iPhone, published under the Google Play developer account Horoscope365 - the controller is a natural person, Zheng Kui, with a Beijing postal address on the Play developer block. You record income, expenses and transfers by hand, by voice ("lunch 12"), by photographing a receipt or bill, or on Android with Premium by confirming a transaction captured from banking or payment app notifications; Premium adds bill import, unlimited AI entry, app lock and extra books. Budgets can be set monthly and per category, with charts, category reports, multiple currencies, separate books, AA split ledgers and shared team books, and data exports to CSV, Excel or PDF. It deliberately does not link to a bank and never asks for bank credentials: without sign-in records stay on the phone, and signing in backs them up to the vendor's own server. Distribution is established rather than nominal - 5M+ Google Play installs at 4.8 stars from roughly 324K reviews, an App Store listing at 4.8 from 414 ratings, both updated in October 2026. The weakness is documentation, not the product: the marketing site publishes no price, links no legal page and prints no contact address, and the only privacy notice sits at an unlinked path that never mentions the financial data, receipt photos, voice clips or notification text the app handles.

pricing: Single price, no tiers and no subscription: USD 6.99 one-time for one 15-second video (portrait 9:16 or landscape 16:9, one of four preset looks, AI-generated synchronised audio, MP4 download). No free tier or trial; the page's samples are the vendor's own renders. Checkout is hosted by Waffo Pancake as merchant of record; applicable tax is shown before payment. The site's own public config endpoint returns price 6.99, currency USD, billing one-time, mode prod - matching /pricing and the homepage.
best_for: Pet owners who want a finished, shareable Halloween video of their own animal and would rather pay $6.99 once than learn a prompt box or a video editor. The preset-look model is the point: four costumes, two aspect ratios, no free-form prompt, no timeline. Not a fit for anyone who wants to direct the scene, needs more than one video for the money, wants a free trial before paying, or needs a named company, postal address or contractual jurisdiction to buy from.
summary: Marigold Pet makes one thing: a 15-second Halloween video of your pet from a single photo. You upload a clear JPG/PNG/WebP up to 10 MB, pick one of four preset looks - pumpkin, witch, vampire or friendly ghost - and either 9:16 or 16:9, pay $6.99 once, and get an MP4 with a three-beat structure (arrival in a Halloween scene, magical costume reveal, hero pose) plus AI-generated synchronised audio. There are no prompts to write and no editing step. Costume stills run on Google Nano Banana 2 and the video and audio on MiniMax H3 Max Turbo, both through fal.ai; each finished video passes the provider's safety checker before delivery. The site is bilingual (English and Spanish) and the interface, pricing and legal pages are served in both languages.
